To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the selection of students to medical school on the basis of the GAMSAT, the interview, and the undergraduate degree is not a good predictor of success in medical school, and that a student’s performance on one exam is not a good indication of performance in another exam.
• The academic record was the only factor consistently correlated with subsequent assessment performance, but it only accounted for 30% of the variance in the exam results.

1) the selection process for graduate entry medical students was not related to performance in subsequent examinations; 2) there was a striking lack in relationships between most selection criteria and subsequent performance; 3) there was a correlation between the General Examination and Academic Selection components; 4) there was no correlation between interview scores and subsequent performance; and 5) the results raise questions about methods of selection and their effectiveness for assessing suitability for a career in medicine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the selection and performance of students on a graduate entry medical course.
the question of what makes a good student and what makes a good physician.
the effectiveness of the current selection and assessment processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive statement to be made.
the present methods are of limited value and that a more holistic approach to selection and assessment is required.
the selection process for graduate entry medicine is not effective in predicting performance and that the assessment process is not effective in identifying unsuitable students.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selection and assessment criteria were not related to performance in the first two years of medical school.
the selection and assessment procedures used here were not effective.
the current selection and assessment methods are not very good at identifying the best students.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many factors that contribute to success, and the best predictor of success is past performance.

selection and assessment procedures should be re-examined to ensure that students are being admitted on the basis of their suitability for the medical profession, rather than their previous academic performance.
there is a need to review the selection and assessment processes for graduate medical students.
